newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: CAMBODIA: EXTRA 3 HERCULES A PRECAUTION
Defence Minister Ian McLachlan has defended the Federal Government against criticism it has been slow to arrange for the evacuation of Australians from Cambodia.
Speaking in Brisbane, Mr McLachlan said Australians in Cambodia are not demanding to be evacuated.
But he says an extra three C-130 Hercules aircraft will arrive in Darwin tonight, along with 90 personnel, in case the situation worsens.

"That's precautionary, if you like. We may or may not need to use them. If we do, the earliest would be Friday and if that's the case it'd be announced by the Foreign Minister or Prime Minister," Mr McLachlan said.
"There's no point in trying to move people out who don't want to go and the fact of the matter is the demand for people to come out is not there so if that demand comes forward we'll be ready to go."

The Australian Defence Force's Colonel Andrew Reynolds said the extra planes are needed because it now appears there are more than 800 Australians in Phnom Penh, an increase on yesterday's estimate of 550.
But Colonel Reynolds also conceded the planes will probably not be necessary.

"It's far better for us to be safe than sorry if you like. The safety of our Australian citizens is paramount in this and if the situation should degrade, it's far better for us to be in a much easier position to help our citizens on the ground," Colonel Reynolds said.
COSTELLO UNDER FIRE OVER GOLD SELL-OFF
The Minerals Council of Australia has questioned whether the Reserve Bank needed to announce its big sell-off of gold.
Council Executive Director, Dick Wells, said the bank's announcement, and the Federal Government's comments, did not have any regard for the broader ramifications of the sale.
Mr Wells said other central banks have sold gold, but without the dramatic effects seen in Australia.

"The Treasurer's comments and the Reserve Bank's statement tended to demean the value of the mineral, gold, in people's minds and has obviously done considerable damage in the markets, which we are seeing," Mr Wells said.
"The fall-out from that won't be evident for probably a month or two yet."
But Mr Wells concedes he has been surprised by the scale of the market reaction to the sell-off.
He said it is difficult to work out the final damages bill to the gold industry.
"It can be a matter of adding up which mines are shutting down, and which new mines may not open up," Mr Wells said.
But he said the Gold Council of Western Australia has estimated job losses in the industry at about 5,000.
The Association of Mining and Exploration Companies is also worried about job losses.
NEW APPOINTEE UNFAZED BY CASA CONTROVERSY
The latest appointee to the Civil Aviation Safety Authority Board, Paul Scully-Power, says he was not put off taking the job by the controversy surrounding the board.
The Federal Government has been pushing to restructure the board, to replace members with people who have direct expertise in the aviation industry.
Dr Scully-Power and former RAAF Wing Commander, Bruce Byron, are the latest appointees, replacing Gabi Hollows and Geoff Molloy.
Dr Scully-Power was Australia's first astronaut, flying on the space shuttle, Challenger, in 1984, and he says his new job is a magnificent opportunity.
"I think it's very much a case of it's time to work together as a team, put a team together and go and do the right thing for aviation in the country," he said.
"I think Australia, certainly in my experience of travelling the world, is a magnificent country for aviation."
SECT IN VICTORIA UNDER POLICE INVESTIGATION
A sect in Central Victoria, allegedly linked to the Branch Davidian group in the United States, is under police investigation.
Detectives are about to hold a media conference, amid allegations that members of the Order of Saint Charbel, living at Tyaak near Seymour, were told to prepare for a Waco-style confrontation.
About 80 members of the Branch Davidian sect died in a fire at Waco Texas in 1993, after a siege with the FBI.
Police will investigate allegations by a 26-year old Victorian man, who's since left the sect, that members here were told to dig graves on their properties in Victoria, and New South Wales.
TABLE SALT COULD REDUCE NEED FOR CHEMICALS: RESEARCHERS
Queensland researchers say they've discovered common table salt reduces by two-thirds the need for some agricultural chemicals.
DPI researchers at Kingaroy, in the South Burnett, have found that by adding salt, some chemicals are just as effective against pests, even though much less is used.
Entomologist Hugh Brier said there are now moves to have salt-enhanced insecticides registered for farm use.
Mr Brier said his work with the chemical, Endosulphan, together with salt has proved effective against a range of pod-sucking insects.
CRICKET: JULIAN SMASHES TON, WARNE SAYS SORRY
Brendan Julian smashed eight sixes in a whirlwind 106 in Australia's nine-run win over the Minor Counties in a one-day match at Jesmond, near Newcastle, in the north of England overnight.
After the match, Julian, who batted at number four, played down his performance, and said the match was played on a small ground.
Julian said he had some lucky hits, "sometimes they come off, sometimes they don't, but it was good to hit a few in the middle".
Julian's Ashes tour team-mate, Shane Warne, has apologised for making a single-fingered gesture to the crowd after Australia's win in the third test.
Warne is on his way back to Australia for a flying visit to his wife and newborn daughter.
Photographs of Warne gesticulating to the Old Trafford crowd have appeared in newspapers around the world.
But he said the gesture was not intended to insult anyone.
